subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = 2S, then prove that cos(S−A) + cos(S−B) + cosC = −1 + 4 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2) cos(C/2).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.42 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 30.2. Printed appearances: TS 17. The twin of 30.1 with cosines throughout. The book calls the pair a "Superb Pairing". The −1 arises exactly as it did in answer 26.2, from choosing cos C = 2cos²(C/2) − 1. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The 1+2+2+1+1 above follows the shape of the split the same book DOES print for LAQ answer 23 on book p.37, weighting the two substantial transformations against the set-up and the finish. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. A student who learns that arc once can attempt any of them. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q23 is the Transformations slot and is ALWAYS a question of this kind.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The same S-condition as its twin — and the same observation, that the two shifted angles add to C.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Two of the seven marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.

recall.must_convey: That the two shifted cosines are paired with the cos C + cos D formula.
accept: pair the first two with cos C plus cos D
apply sum to product to the two shifted cosines
combine cos S minus A and cos S minus B
modati rendu cosines ni combine cheyyali
use the cosine sum formula on the pair

steps.why: Identical opening to the twin question — only the formula changes from sine to cosine.
common_mistakes: Using the sine formula by habit.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.

recall.must_convey: That 2S − (A+B) becomes C, and cos C is expanded as 2cos²(C/2) − 1 — producing the −1 and a shared cos(C/2).
accept: the half sum becomes C over two and cos C is two cos squared half C minus one which gives the minus one
expand cos C in half angles so both terms carry cos C over two
the minus one comes from the double angle expansion
cos C ni two cos square C by two minus one ga rasta, minus one vasthundi
substitute and expand to get the common factor

steps.why: Choosing 2cos²(θ/2) − 1 rather than 1 − 2sin²(θ/2) is deliberate: it produces both the −1 the answer needs and a cos(C/2) that matches the other term.
common_mistakes: Using the sine form and getting +1 with sines that will not factor.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.

recall.must_convey: That −1 is set aside, 2 cos(C/2) taken out, and cos(C/2) rewritten in the shifted angles.
accept: separate the minus one, take two cos C over two common, then convert C back to S minus A plus S minus B
set the minus one aside and factor out two cos half C
the bracket becomes two cosines in the shifted angles
minus one veru chesi two cos C by two common teeyyali
rewrite the bracket in S minus A and S minus B

steps.why: Setting the constant aside before factoring is the same tactic used in answers 26.2 and 28 — it keeps the line short and the common factor visible.
common_mistakes: Trying to factor the −1 into the bracket.
Leaving the bracket in terms of C.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.

recall.must_convey: That the sum of cosines becomes 2 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2), giving −1 + 4 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2) cos(C/2).
accept: the sum gives two cos half S minus A cos half S minus B so the answer is minus one plus four of those times cos half C
apply the cosine sum formula and keep the minus one
the answer is minus one plus four cos cos cos
minus one plus four cos half S minus A cos half S minus B cos half C
finish with the cosine sum formula

steps.why: Every factor in this answer is a cosine, where its twin finished with a sine. The difference traces back to one choice made three steps earlier.
common_mistakes: Finishing with sin(C/2) by copying the twin.
